chapters.title: The question hidden in two boards
narration: A 2V dome does not ask its two strut classes to be in the golden ratio.
It inherits phi in the parent icosahedron, then changes the edge geometry
when straight midpoints are projected back to a sphere.

chapters.title: Why domes triangulate
narration: Push the top node: the force resolves into axial paths along the edges.
Triangulation trades bending-prone panels for a network of tension and
compression members. Real joints and foundations still require engineering.

chapters.title: The five regular starting points
narration: Each Platonic solid has one regular face type and one vertex arrangement.
More evenly distributed vertices mean a smaller correction when we project
the surface outward. The icosahedron gives twenty equilateral launch pads.

chapters.title: Where the golden ratio really lives
narration: The coordinate families (0, ±1, ±phi), (±1, ±phi, 0), and
(±phi, 0, ±1) place twelve points at one common radius.
Any neighboring pair is exactly 2 units apart before normalization.

chapters.title: Put the icosahedron on a unit sphere
narration: Normalize each vertex by its distance from the origin.
Now the sphere radius is exactly one. Every measured edge is a multiplier
that can later be scaled to inches, feet, meters, or any other unit.

chapters.title: Split every parent edge in half
narration: The arithmetic midpoint is easy: average the two endpoint vectors.
But that point lies inside the sphere. Leaving it there makes a faceted
icosahedron subdivision—not a geodesic sphere.

chapters.title: Project the midpoints outward
narration: Each midpoint travels on a ray from the origin until its radius is one.
The new point changes the chord distances inside every subdivided face.
That single operation is where the two finished lengths appear.

chapters.title: Measure and group every chord
narration: SHORT connects a parent vertex to a projected midpoint.
LONG connects two projected midpoints. Color grouping is numerical:
equal lengths receive equal colors—no letter convention is required.

chapters.title: Four routes to the same answer
narration: Coordinate route: subtract endpoint vectors and take the magnitude.
Angle route: theta = acos(u dot v), then chord = 2R sin(theta/2).
Law of cosines, a spreadsheet, Python, and CAD must reproduce the same values.

chapters.title: Audit the 72 in / 63.5 in dome
narration: Use each member independently to estimate radius, then use a least-squares
fit when both measurements contain cutting, hub, or tape error.
Center-to-center geometry must be separated from physical cut length.

chapters.title: From radius to a cut list
narration: A hemisphere contains 65 unique structural edges and 40 triangular faces.
The theoretical lengths are hub-center to hub-center. Tube, timber, tabs,
and commercial hubs each need their own verified end allowance.

chapters.title: Panels, hubs, and build sequence
narration: Make full-size gauges for SHORT and LONG, batch-cut, and label every part.
Dry-build repeating triangles before raising rings from the base upward.
PVC, timber, and tube share centerlines—not end cuts or structural capacity.

chapters.title: Close the measurement loop
narration: Check member gauges, base decagon diagonals, hub-center radius, and level.
Small repeated errors accumulate around a ring. Correct them before the apex.
For occupied or load-bearing structures, use local code and an engineer.

chapters.title: The whole transformation
narration: Raw phi coordinates become a normalized icosahedron.
Midpoints move outward, two chord factors emerge, and one scale factor
turns the unit geometry into a buildable 2V dome.

chapters.title: Do the one thing
narration: If any of this was worth your time, send it to one person who can
carry it further than I can. That is the whole ask. One share from
somebody with reach does more for this than a month of me in a field
with a chainsaw.
